memoryText: But as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD.
memoryVerseMeditation:
Today there is no new reading. Today is for review and reflection on what you have learned in Unit 8.

Begin by memorizing the verse above if you have not already. Joshua 24:15 comes at the end of a long speech, and the whole of Judges shows what happens when it is forgotten. Say it aloud several times. Notice three things.

First, “But as for me.” The sentence begins with a contrast. Others may choose differently. The gods of the Amorites and the gods beyond the river are all available. Joshua does not pretend there are no options, and he does not wait to see what the crowd decides. He makes a personal commitment.

Second, “and my house.” The commitment extends to the household. Joshua takes responsibility for the spiritual direction of those under his care. This does not mean he can force their faith, but he will lead, teach, and set an example. The failure of the generation after Joshua is the failure to pass this on.

Third, “we will serve the LORD.” The verb is “serve,” meaning worship and obey. It is not a vague spirituality but a covenant loyalty. And the one served has a name: the LORD, who rescued Israel from Egypt and gave them the land. Joshua will go on to say that the people cannot do this in their own strength. We cannot either. The strength to serve is given by Christ. Pray this verse over your home, your relationships, and your calling.
unitRecap:
In Unit 8 you have traveled through Joshua, Judges, and Ruth, the story of Israel’s entry into the land and the long, painful years that followed. The unit began with God’s commission to Joshua and the promise of his presence. You met Rahab, a Canaanite woman who confessed that the LORD is God, hung a scarlet cord, and was brought into the line of the Messiah. You watched the priests step into the Jordan, and you saw twelve stones piled up as a memorial. You saw Jericho fall by faith and obedience, and Israel stumble at Ai because of Achan’s hidden sin. You read about the Gibeonite deception, the day the sun stood still, and the northern campaign.

You then studied the distribution of the land: Caleb’s faithfulness at eighty-five, the Levites whose inheritance was the LORD himself, the survey of the remaining territory, the cities of refuge that point to Christ our refuge, and the near-war over the altar that was settled by Phinehas’s careful inquiry. You heard Joshua’s farewell and the great call, “Choose this day whom you will serve,” along with the sober reminder that no one is able to serve a holy God in his own strength.

Judges opened with the incomplete conquest and the generation that did not know the LORD. You followed the repeating cycle of sin, oppression, cry, and rescue through Othniel, Ehud, Deborah and Barak, Gideon, Abimelech, Jephthah, and Samson. You saw how each judge was flawed, and how the nation slid toward idolatry and violence. The last chapters showed a people doing what was right in their own eyes, with the refrain “no king in Israel.” Then Ruth lit a lamp in the dark: a Moabite widow who took refuge under the wings of the LORD, and a redeemer named Boaz who became the great-grandfather of King David.

Along the way, the Psalms gave you words for every season: the sea fleeing in Psalm 114, God’s testing in Psalm 66, your portion in Psalm 16, the shepherd of Psalm 23, the refuge of Psalm 46, the warrior-judge of Psalm 76, the depths of Psalm 130, the new song of Psalm 40, and the house built by the LORD in Psalms 127 and 128.

The message of the unit is that God keeps his promises even when his people do not. The rest he gives is partial and fragile, and it points forward to a better Joshua, a better king, and a better Redeemer.

reviewQuestions.question: What does the conquest reveal about the holiness and justice of God?
reviewQuestions.prompt: Look back at Jericho, Achan, and the Gibeonites. The conquest was a judgment on nations whose sin had reached its full measure (Genesis 15:16), and it also showed that Israel itself was not exempt. Achan’s sin brought judgment on Israel, and Rahab’s faith brought rescue to a Canaanite. God’s holiness is real, and his mercy reaches those who take refuge in him. Write a few sentences about how these chapters help you hold God’s justice and mercy together. How does the cross, where judgment and mercy meet, bring this tension to its resolution?

reviewQuestions.question: What is the cycle in Judges, and how does it function as a mirror for our own hearts?
reviewQuestions.prompt: Recall the pattern: Israel did evil, God gave them into the hands of oppressors, they cried out, God raised up a deliverer, there was rest, and then they relapsed. The judges themselves were flawed, and the book ends in moral chaos. Look at your own life. Where do you see a similar pattern of forgetting, trouble, crying out, and rescue? How does the book make you long for a better deliverer? Write down how Christ breaks the cycle in a way the judges could not.

reviewQuestions.question: How does Rahab’s story illustrate justification by faith?
reviewQuestions.prompt: Reread Joshua 2 and compare it with Hebrews 11:31 and James 2:25. Rahab was a Canaanite and a prostitute, outside the covenant, with no works to boast of. She heard what God had done, believed, and took refuge in the way of rescue he provided. The scarlet cord marked her house. She was saved by faith, and her actions showed her faith was real. Think about how her story anticipates the gospel. How does it clarify the relationship between faith, works, and the grace of God in Christ?

reviewQuestions.question: How does Boaz function as a kinsman-redeemer, and how does he point to Christ?
reviewQuestions.prompt: Return to Ruth 3-4. A redeemer had to be a relative, able to pay the price, and willing to do so. Boaz fulfilled all three. Jesus became our brother in flesh and blood, paid the price of his own life, and did so willingly, for the joy set before him. Consider your own story. What debts or burdens have you been unable to pay? Write a short prayer of thanks to Christ, your Redeemer, for what he has done on your behalf.

prayerPrompts: Thank God for keeping every promise and going before his people.
Confess where you have done what is right in your own eyes.
Ask him to keep the unit verse before you.
